name: Liothyronine
summary: Synthetic triiodothyronine (T3), the directly active thyroid hormone, used when rapid onset is needed or as an adjunct in selected hypothyroidism.
mechanism: Binds nuclear thyroid hormone receptors directly as the active hormone, regulating gene transcription without requiring peripheral conversion.
pharmacodynamics: Raises metabolic rate and tissue T3 rapidly; short half-life means levels fluctuate more than with T4.

dosing.adult: 25–75 mcg/day in divided doses as adjunct or alternative; IV in myxedema coma

safety.pregnancy: Not preferred for maintenance; T4-based therapy is standard in pregnancy
safety.lactation: Caution with high doses; monitor infant
warnings: Rapid onset/offset causes fluctuating hormone levels
Cardiac effects (tachycardia, atrial fibrillation) with over-replacement
safety.overdose: Thyrotoxic symptoms; supportive care, beta-blockers for adrenergic symptoms

indications: Hypothyroidism as alternative or adjunct to T4 (selected cases, e.g., persistent symptoms on T4 alone)
Myxedema coma (IV, with T4 or alone)
clinicalPearls: The short half-life means missed doses cause rapid swings — adherence and divided dosing matter.
Rarely used as monotherapy for maintenance; most patients do best on T4 alone.
good: Fast onset when rapid correction is needed (e.g., myxedema coma).
bad: Fluctuating levels, cardiac risk in susceptible patients, and more intensive monitoring.
